The WHO, in collaboration with the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the High-Risk Unaffected Countries Team of the International Task Force for the 2014 Ebola Response, developed an emergency guideline for implementing and managing contact tracing for Ebola Virus Disease (EVD). This guideline is based on a document titled Contact Tracing During an Outbreak of Ebola Virus Disease, created by the Disease Surveillance and Response Programme of the WHO African Region (AFRO). The guideline was developed with contributions from numerous experts and organizations. EVD is transmissible as soon as symptoms appear, making it critical to identify and isolate symptomatic individuals immediately to prevent further spread. Contact tracing is a vital tool for breaking chains of transmission and controlling EVD outbreaks. It involves identifying, assessing, and managing individuals exposed to the disease to prevent onward transmission. Exposed individuals are systematically monitored for 21 days, the maximum incubation period for EVD, to quickly identify and isolate symptomatic cases. Prompt isolation and treatment also improve survival rates by reducing delays in supportive care. Previous EVD outbreaks have demonstrated the effectiveness of contact tracing in halting transmission. However, during the 2014 West Africa outbreak, contact tracing faced significant challenges, including the wide geographic spread of the outbreak (involving both urban and rural areas), insufficient resources (human, financial, and logistical), community resistance, and limited access to affected communities. The lack of standardized procedures for implementing and managing contact tracing led to delays and inefficiencies, contributing to ongoing transmission. This operational document provides guidance for implementing and managing contact tracing in countries preparing for or responding to EVD outbreaks. It addresses common challenges and offers potential solutions, as well as guidance on monitoring and evaluating the contact tracing process. The guide is based on best practices from previous EVD outbreaks and the 2014 West Africa outbreak. The target audience for this guide includes national and sub-national emergency management committees, epidemiologists, surveillance officers, and volunteer organizations involved in EVD preparedness and response activities. It is intended to help these groups plan, implement, and manage contact tracing efforts, with adaptations to local contexts as needed. Contact tracing is a critical component of EVD outbreak control but is only one part of a multifaceted response strategy. It is closely linked to case finding (surveillance) and case investigation processes. Detecting an EVD case triggers case investigation, during which contacts are identified, initiating the contact tracing process. These efforts rely on other aspects of the EVD response, such as social mobilization, logistics, case management, and laboratory capacity. Effective contact tracing requires immediate implementation after case detection and efficient management, necessitating comprehensive preparation and coordination across all response activities. For contact tracing to be effective, active participation and cooperation from affected communities are essential. Building trust between public health officials and the community is critical. Early engagement of key community members, stakeholders, and volunteers in response planning fosters community ownership and trust in the health system. Communities must feel confident in cooperating with teams conducting case investigations and contact tracing and supporting the referral of symptomatic contacts to designated isolation and treatment facilities. Effective communication and culturally sensitive messaging are crucial to avoid counterproductive practices and stigma. Public misinterpretations of contact lists as lists of individuals likely to die can lead to resistance and hinder contact tracing efforts. Therefore, health communication, messaging, and psychosocial support are vital. Social mobilization and community engagement are critical to the success of contact tracing. Successful contact tracing requires skills in assessing EVD symptoms, interviewing techniques, and counseling. Contact tracers must have investigative skills to identify and track all potential contacts and the ability to analyze evidence. They must also be flexible and empathetic to build trust with cases, contacts, and their families. Insufficient expertise or failure to consider individual, community, social, cultural, and religious sensitivities can alienate individuals and communities, undermining contact tracing efforts. However, contact tracing activities can also provide opportunities to establish strong community partnerships. The implementation of contact tracing activities may vary depending on the disease burden and local context. In areas with a high number of EVD cases and contacts, logistical challenges may arise in locating and tracing all individuals exposed to a case. Comprehensive and systematic contact tracing efforts must be supported by robust community engagement and intensified social mobilization. Active case finding should also be conducted in conjunction with contact tracing to detect other symptomatic individuals in defined areas. Effective contact tracing requires strict adherence to definitions of contact and EVD case to promptly identify all contacts and cases. Failure to apply correct definitions can result in ongoing transmission. Developing a local definition of an EVD alert with less stringent criteria than an EVD case may help detect infected individuals earlier. All alerts should be investigated to determine whether they meet the EVD case definition. Contacts are individuals exposed to a suspected, probable, or confirmed EVD case in specific ways, such as living in the same household, having direct physical contact with the case (alive or deceased), participating in funeral or burial rituals, or coming into contact with the case's blood or body fluids. Health workers involved in patient care, cleaning, waste management, or laboratory work are also considered contacts. Delays in response can lead to rapid disease spread, making preparation essential. This includes identifying and allocating the necessary infrastructure, personnel, resources, and funding before the first EVD case is detected.
